clue.text: Dog ran off with fisherman's bait — this creature!

indicators.note: off suggests the two words have gone wrong or bad, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: an angler's artificial bait is a fly

explanation.surface: An angler's dog bolts with his bait, and we are invited to marvel at some creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this creature!' is the definition, pointing at an insect; the dog in the surface is only anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation points at an insect of the order Odonata, the long-bodied darter of ponds.

clue.text: Right in the middle of the cemetery?

definitions.text: Right in the middle of the cemetery?

parts.words: Right in the middle of the cemetery?
parts.note: the phrase for exactly in the middle is read literally as the very centre of the place where the departed lie

explanation.surface: Someone asks for the precise midpoint of a graveyard.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means precisely central; a cemetery's middle is literally a centre of the departed.

clue.text: Often, so to speak, inside the pale

definitions.text: Often, so to speak, inside the pale

parts.words: Often, so to speak, inside the pale
parts.note: pallid people frequently have this blood condition within them, with a nod to the old fenced boundary called the Pale

explanation.surface: It reads like a remark about life within the old English enclave in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the pale' looks like the historical Pale, an enclosed district; it means people who look pale, and the condition is often found inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: A shortage of red blood cells or haemoglobin commonly causes pallor, so it often lies within those who look wan.

clue.text: In good condition — a gentle one, this animal

parts.note: OK means all right, in good shape
PI, short for pious, describes a mild, goody-goody person

explanation.surface: A healthy, docile animal is presented to us.
explanation.definitionFit: The animal meant is the shy striped-legged relative of the giraffe from the Congo forests.

clue.text: Toys with absurd digital protection device

parts.note: to toy with something is to finger it idly
tall, as in a tall story, means far-fetched

explanation.surface: Someone fiddles with a ridiculous gadget for guarding something electronic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digital' looks electronic but refers to the digits of the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheath worn over an injured finger is a guard for a digit.

clue.text: Isle of Wight banker raising the beam

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word means writing it upwards, so it reads backwards

parts.note: a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: A bank employee on the Isle of Wight lifts a wooden beam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banker' is not a financier but something with banks, a river; the Yar flows on the Isle of Wight, an island off England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A river has banks, so it is jokingly a banker; this one runs through the Isle of Wight.

clue.text: Secret store of money that has been uttered

indicators.note: uttered means spoken aloud, so the word for money is heard rather than seen

parts.note: cash is money in notes and coins

explanation.surface: A hidden hoard of coins has been passed off, as in uttering forged notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uttered' also means passing counterfeit money, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden hoard of supplies or valuables is a hiding place's contents.

clue.text: Diversion of rich variety, yet unnecessary for mock serenade

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Diversion of rich variety, yet unnecessary for mock serenade' (9): RICH VARIETY less YET leaves RICHVARI, one A short of CHARIVARI; a composite-anagram setter slip the check cannot record, and no printed source found to show a dropped 'a'
annotationWithheld.clue: Diversion of rich variety, yet unnecessary for mock serenade

clue.text: European wine although it turns up from China, strangely

indicators.note: strangely says the letters of China appear in an odd order
in a down clue, turning up a word reads it bottom to top, so backwards

explanation.surface: A European wine is surprisingly found arriving from China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strangely' rearranges CHINA into CHIAN; 'turns up' writes IT backwards as TI below it.
explanation.definitionFit: The red wine of Tuscany in Italy is a European vintage.

clue.text: They may look right to superiors

definitions.text: They may look right to superiors

parts.words: They may look right to superiors
parts.note: on parade the command to turn the gaze to the right is a salute to a senior officer

explanation.surface: It seems to describe subordinates who appear correct to their bosses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'look right' seems to mean appear correct; it is literally turning the gaze rightwards, as in the parade-ground salute.
explanation.definitionFit: These organs of sight are what soldiers turn rightward to salute a passing officer.

clue.text: Reptile in bag a man carried

indicators.note: the bag carries the creature within the run of its words

explanation.surface: A man carries a reptile around in his bag.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a kind of Old World lizard.

clue.text: English girl has German girl to bring within limits

parts.note: Norma is a girl's name used in England
Lise is a German girl's name, a form of Elisabeth

explanation.surface: An English girl lodges a German girl to keep her in line.
explanation.definitionFit: To regularise or standardise is to keep within accepted bounds.

clue.text: Rome's in atomic disaster evoking pity

indicators.note: a disaster wrecks things, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A nuclear catastrophe in Rome arouses sympathy.
explanation.definitionFit: Sympathy expressed for someone's misfortune is a synonym for pity.

clue.text: Befitting to steal?

explanation.surface: A pun on whether stealing is ever suitable.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means suitable or fitting; as a verb, to take for oneself without right.

clue.text: Recoil at return of psychiatrist

parts.note: shrink is slang for a psychiatrist, from headshrinker
to go back is to return

explanation.surface: Someone flinches when the psychiatrist comes back.
explanation.definitionFit: To flinch or draw away in fear is a phrasal verb meaning recoil.

clue.text: Suspicion of a nuns' frolic, around the church

indicators.note: around says the scrambled letters go round the abbreviation for the church
a frolic is a romp, so the letters caper about into a new order

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone hints that a convent's nuns have been up to mischief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspicion' here means a faint trace, as in a suspicion of garlic, not mistrust of the nuns.
explanation.definitionFit: A suspicion in the sense of a faint trace or hint matches a subtle shade of meaning.

clue.text: Compel to study ancestry

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
a strain is a line of descent or breed

explanation.surface: Someone is driven to research their family tree.
explanation.definitionFit: To force or oblige someone is a synonym for compel.

clue.text: Hammer and polish metal. Following design is hard

indicators.note: following says the words after it come next in line, after the design

parts.note: a plan is a design or scheme
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A metalworker's instructions: beat and buff the metal, though the design is tricky.
explanation.definitionFit: This metalworking verb means to flatten and smooth sheet metal by light hammering.

clue.text: Do a turn, waltzing round building

indicators.note: waltzing whirls the letters round into a new order

explanation.surface: Dancers twirl around a building while waltzing.
explanation.definitionFit: A circular building, especially one with a dome, is a round structure.

clue.text: Providing information that's of significance

explanation.surface: A double definition: giving news, and being revealing.
explanation.definitionFit: It can mean relating or narrating facts, and also striking or revealing, as a remark that counts.

clue.text: Japanese paper folding, but there's no job loss involved

definitions.text: Japanese paper folding, but there's no job loss involved

parts.words: Japanese paper folding, but there's no job loss involved
parts.note: a newspaper folding means it closes down and staff are laid off, but this kind of folding paper is a craft

explanation.surface: It reads like news of a Japanese newspaper closing without redundancies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paper folding' looks like a newspaper going out of business; here it is the craft of creasing paper into shapes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese art of making figures by creasing sheets of paper is the craft described.

clue.text: Suffer tortuous agonies

indicators.note: tortuous means twisting, so the letters are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone endures twisted torments.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in torment or anguish over something is to suffer.

clue.text: Former Oriental leader's published work not often consulted, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the phrase is taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: a book that is seldom read is a little-read book

explanation.surface: A one-time Chinese chairman's writings are said to be rarely opened.
explanation.walkthrough: Mao Zedong, former leader of China, was author of the famous book of quotations; 'read' in the past tense sounds like the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Mao's collected quotations, waved by Red Guards, are the work of a former Chinese leader.

clue.text: Quaffed by rating on quarterdeck

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another sits beneath it, so the rating goes below

parts.note: a quarter of the four-letter word deck is its first letter
a rating is a rank or grade

explanation.surface: A sailor of low rating knocks back a drink on the ship's quarterdeck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarterdeck' is read as quarter of deck, one of its four letters, D.
explanation.definitionFit: Quaffed means gulped down a drink, the past tense of a verb of swallowing.

clue.text: River flowing through the Bronte country

indicators.note: the river flows through the run of these words, lying within them

explanation.surface: A river runs through the Yorkshire moors associated with the Bronte sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bronte country is the Yorkshire moorland of the novelist sisters; the river is in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a major river of north-east Spain.

clue.text: Train in a bank, initially, to become our sitting representative

indicators.note: initially takes just the opening letter of the word bank
the letters are changed so as to become a new word

explanation.surface: A trainee in a bank aims to become a Member of Parliament, the people's sitting representative.
explanation.walkthrough: Britannia, the figure personifying Britain, is shown seated on British coins, hence 'sitting'.
explanation.definitionFit: The seated female figure on British coinage personifies the nation, so she represents us.

clue.text: The point of giving up food

indicators.note: in a down clue, giving up means sending the word upward, so it reads backwards

parts.note: a bun is a small item of food

explanation.surface: Someone asks what the purpose of dieting is.
explanation.definitionFit: The crux or gist of a matter is its central point.

clue.text: Two articles a girl produced

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Two articles a girl produced' (5): AN and A are articles but nothing fairly gives the IT in ANITA, and the clue could not be found in print to check for a misread

clue.text: House journal with a lofty tone?

explanation.surface: A company magazine is accused of a superior manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lofty tone' sounds like snobbery but refers to the instrument's pipes sounding high in a church.
explanation.definitionFit: A periodical speaking for a body is its mouthpiece, and the pipe instrument in church makes high-pitched music.

clue.text: Crack bottle — where it's corked — at high speed

parts.note: to break something is to crack it
the cork goes into the narrow top part of a bottle

explanation.surface: Someone smashes a bottle at the corked end in a great hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: Dangerously fast, as if risking a fractured spine, describes headlong speed.
